items.name: Aurora — adjudication
items.description: Claims system of record.

replication.notes: Aurora Global Database: us-east-1 primary, us-east-2 secondary, storage-level async replication. A planned switchover is RPO 0; an UNPLANNED failover loses whatever had not shipped — typically well under a second of writes. Quote the unplanned figure. 1 minute is recorded as a conservative ceiling; the number to put in a test record is the measured replica lag at T0 (AuroraGlobalDBReplicationLag). Aurora PostgreSQL can enforce a ceiling with rds.global_db_rpo, which blocks commits when lag exceeds it.

verification.pass: connect + query OK from recovered app pod

items.notes: The secondary is kept small and is scaled up at failover — managed failover is "order of minutes", not seconds, and the scale-up is part of the RTA. Verify the secondary's instance class against full production load before trusting the number.

items.name: Aurora — pricing
items.description: Pricing reference data.

replication.notes: AWS Backup cross-region copy, daily. Deliberate: pricing reference data is reloaded from the drug-price feed on a weekly cycle, so the RPO here is the backup cadence (24 h) and a global cluster would buy nothing. Copies are re-encrypted with the destination vault key, so the recovery-region vault key has to exist first.

verification.pass: a copied recovery point for the pricing cluster dated within 24 h

items.notes: A store whose RPO is a day is a decision, not an oversight — it is written down here so nobody has to re-derive it during an event.

items.name: Aurora — remittance
items.description: Remittance/settlement records.

replication.notes: THIRD-PARTY: recovered from Arpio recovery points (snapshot-based point-in-time recovery), configured at 30 min. This is the one Tier-0 store still on point-in-time recovery rather than continuous replication, and it is the one that missed — test #2 measured a 118-min RPA against the 30-min configuration because the recovery points were not aligned across stores. Kept here on purpose as the contrast with cmp_aurora_adj: snapshot recovery gives you a consistent moment, not a current one. Migration to Aurora Global Database is the open item in dec_mechanisms.

verification.command: psql from a pod: SELECT now() - max(settled_at) FROM remittances
verification.pass: connects, and the age at T0 is recorded as the measured RPA

gaps: Measured RPA of 118 min against a 30-min configured recovery point — points were not aligned across stores (gap_rpa1)

items.name: Secrets Manager (~50 explicit ARNs)
items.description: Runtime secrets consumed by secrets-init at pod start. The single most common cause of failed recovery tests.

replication.notes: Replica secrets in us-east-2. The replica keeps the SAME NAME (only the region in the ARN differs), so name-based lookup fails over cleanly, and rotation propagates to replicas automatically. Propagation is event-driven — 1 min is a conservative ceiling, not a lag budget. The failure mode here is not lag, it is list drift: a secret nobody marked for replication simply is not there, and every replica needs a KMS key in the recovery region to decrypt with. Three lists still disagree (replica-enabled secrets, the manual spreadsheet, the runtime logical names) — that is what killed test #2.

verification.command: secrets-init logs clean; every runtime logical name resolves
verification.pass: no ResourceNotFoundException on any logical name

gaps: Secret lists disagree — reconcile into one signed-off CSV of logical names, then verify each one is replicated

replication.notes: Native ECR cross-region replication rules at registry level; AWS states the majority of images replicate in under 30 min. Two traps: only images pushed AFTER the rule was created are replicated (the backlog has to be re-pushed), and repository settings and lifecycle policies are NOT replicated — recreate those with IaC. A pull-through cache rule needs an internet path on first pull, so pre-replicate rather than relying on it in an isolated drill.

items.notes:
UNASSIGNED (environment and service): the registry lives in the shared ops account and every environment pulls from it — dev pulled from it during test #2, and production pulls from it at every deploy. Nobody has decided whether it belongs to production's platform service or to a shared-services environment of its own, and guessing would put a Tier-0 dependency in the wrong DR package. The registry is the first thing to prove: a pod that cannot pull is an L4 symptom with an L1 cause. Verify both that the repositories exist and that a pod-identity pull actually succeeds.
